content: The umbilical artery is a paired structure, with one artery present on each side of the body. It is located in the abdominal and pelvic regions and, in the fetus, extends into the umbilical cord. In the fetus, the umbilical arteries are responsible for transporting deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta via the umbilical cord. Typically, there are two umbilical arteries present alongside one umbilical vein within the cord. These arteries are branches of the internal iliac arteries, which supply blood to the hind limbs in the fetus. The umbilical arteries encircle the urinary bladder and carry all deoxygenated blood out of the fetus through the umbilical cord. Notably, the umbilical artery is one of the only arteries in the human body, aside from the pulmonary arteries, that carries deoxygenated blood. Occasionally, only a single umbilical artery (SUA) is present in the umbilical cord. This anomaly is more commonly observed in multiple births but can also occur in singleton pregnancies. Infants with SUA may have an increased likelihood of other congenital abnormalities. However, advanced diagnostic tools, such as high-resolution ultrasound scans, can help rule out these abnormalities before birth, providing reassurance to parents. Genetic counseling may also be beneficial, particularly when considering more invasive diagnostic procedures like chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. It is important to emphasize that a diagnosis of SUA does not necessarily indicate that the fetus is at risk for other complications, either in utero or after birth. Encouragingly, cases where no additional markers for congenital abnormalities are detected via ultrasound are associated with favorable outcomes. Medical literature suggests that SUA occurs in approximately 1 in 100 newborns, making it the most common umbilical cord abnormality. Before the advent of ultrasound technology, SUA could only be identified at birth through examination of the placenta. Even today, many cases of SUA may go undetected antenatally, as most expectant mothers do not undergo the advanced ultrasound imaging required to confirm its presence. In the United States, healthcare providers often recommend regular growth scans near term for pregnancies with SUA to monitor for potential intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), which can occasionally occur and may require intervention. However, most growth-restricted infants with SUA also present with other defects. Late-pregnancy echocardiograms may be advised to ensure proper cardiac function. Additionally, neonates with SUA may have a higher incidence of kidney abnormalities, warranting close examination of the infant shortly after birth. Among SUA infants, there is also a slightly increased risk of postnatal urinary tract infections. In adults, the umbilical artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and represents the patent (open) portion of the embryonic umbilical artery. The obliterated, non-patent portion of the artery becomes the medial umbilical ligament. The umbilical artery is located in the pelvis and gives rise to the superior vesical arteries. In males, it also gives rise to the artery supplying the ductus deferens.
